text: Development of an isothermal reverse transcriptase‑recombinase polymerase amplification assay for the rapid diagnosis of four viroids in different grape cultivars
Pankhuri Singhal1 · Damini Diksha1 · Nishant Srivastava1 · Virendra Kumar Baranwal1
Received: 19 September 2023 / Revised: 19 April 2024 / Accepted: 24 April 2024 © Indian Phytopathological Society 2024

Rapid, isothermal detection is possible using recombinase polymerase amplification assay (RPA) offering great specificity plus sensitivity. An RPA assay was standardized and evaluated to detect four viroids using RNA from infected grapevine plants. From the sequences of the whole genome of four viroids, four pairs of oligonucleotide primers were created. The four viroids employed in this study included Grapevine yellow speckle viroid 1 and 2 (GYSVd-1; GYSVd-2), Australian grapevine viroid (AGVd) and Hop stunt viroid (HSVd). The primers were tested to function both in RPA in addition to polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Applying the RT-RPA assay, the presence of four viroids was determined in a total of 119 symptomatic and asymptomatic grapevine leaf samples from several 22 genotypes obtained from the various regions of India. The results of RT-RPA were compatible with RT-PCR-based detection utilising pure RNA generated cDNA as a template. GYSVd-2 was effectively detected using crude leaf sap in RPA as well. To our awareness, this is the earliest report of consistent diagnosis of most grapevine viroids infection by RT-RPA using RNA as well as crude leaf sap as a template.
Keywords Grapevine Leaf · RNA template, Crude Leaf Extract · Reverse Transcriptase-Polymerase Chain Reaction · Reverse Transcriptase-Recombinase Polymerase Amplification

In terms of productivity, grapevine is India's fifth-largest fruit crop. Known grapevine infections include 67 viruses and 6 viroids, which are known to cause losses in both table and wine grapevine. These infections also lower vine quality and limit production (Basso et al. 2017). Six viroids have been identified as grapevine pathogens globally. Indian grapevines have been the host of five out of the six viroids that have been reported globally viz., Australian grapevine viroid (AGVd) (Adkar-Purushothama et al. 2014), Grapevine yellow speckle viroid-2 (GYSVd-2) (Singhal et al. 2019a, b), Hop stunt viroid (HSVd) and Grapevine yellow speckle viroid-1 (GYSVd-1) (Sahana et al. 2013) and Grapevine
latent viroid (GLVd) (Sidharthan et al. 2020). With the

exception of GYSVd-1 and GYSVd-2, which manifest signs of vein banding and yellow speckle at higher temperatures, the majority of these viroids do not cause any symptoms (Taylor and Woodham 1972). However, in some instances, combined infections of some viruses and particular grapevine-infecting viroids can cause disease. For instance, concurrent infections by the GYSVd-1 and Grapevine Fan Leaf Virus can cause severe vein banding disease (Szychowski et al. 1998). Grapevine viroid transmission is known to occur by infected propagating material during grafting (Szychowski et al. 1988), seeds (Wah and Symons 1999) and mechanical inoculation during the routine cultural practices (Szychowski et al. 1988). However, recent studies on the transmission of viroids in two vineyards do not support their transmission by routine pruning (Staub et al. 1995). While the viroids infection alone causes moderate economic damage to grapevine (Randles 2003), HSVd has been severely damaging to hop production in many areas

Due to certain of their properties, viroids have different diagnostics from viruses. It is difficult to separate viroids
from polysaccharides and polyphenols due to their presence

in small concentrations in plants, are localised in the cell nucleolus, which also houses other large molecules, and lack a protein coat, making protein-based diagnostics inapplicable (Singhal et al. 2021b). Also, infections of viroids along with a number of viruses in mixed infections make things all the more difficult (Singhal et al. 2021a). The same is the case with grapevine and therefore it becomes extremely important for rapid yet specific detection of
viroids for efficient diagnosis of the infection.

Initially the viroids were detected using R-PAGE, after which nucleic acid probe methods came like nucleic acid hybridization and dot blot hybridization, which was 8–10 times more sensitive than polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) and 4–6 times more sensitive than Return-PAGE (R-PAGE) followed by Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). Reverse Transcriptase-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) was used first for detecting viroids in pome fruits in 1990 (Hadidi and Yang 1990), and since then, it has been the most commonly used method for detecting viroids. The need for high-quality nucleic acids as the starting point, the need for a priced thermal cycler, and the strict requirements for thermal cycling are a few of the restrictions that these approaches still face. Additionally, PCR experiments take a fair amount of time (7–8 h) and need an experienced operator. In recent years, a number of diverse amplification techniques based on isothermal conditions utilizing various enzyme processes have been created of which recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA), has proved to be extremely efficient in rapid diagnostics. RPA is an isothermal substitute for PCR that can be carried out in a single tube. Without prior nucleic acid purification, RPA is quick, highly specific, and can identify a single copy of DNA and 10 copies or less of RNA in complex types with just a single primer combination. Only a few nucleic acid molecules can be amplified to a detectable level in 10–20 min while operating at low temperatures of 37–42 °C. It was first introduced in 2006 by Piepenburg et al., engaging DNA for detection by means of recombination proteins. Little Cherry Virus 2 (Mekuria et al. 2014), tomato chlorotic dwarf viroid (TCDVd) (Hammond and Zhang 2016), and HSVd in hop plants (Kappagantu et al. 2017) were detected for the first time using reverse transcriptase-recombinase polymerase chain amplification (RT-RPA) with plant extract as a

To develop a simplified, rapid, sensitive yet specific diagnostic tool for grapevine viroid detection, RPA primer pairs were drafted for the detection of each viroid, and the RT-RPA assay was standardized and the results of which are presented here. The twenty-two genotypes of grapevine used in this study were initially verified for the existence of the grapevine viroids via RT-PCR (Singhal et al. 2019a,
b). This study will be used for accurate yet rapid detection
of grapevine viroids worldwide especially for quick
Survey, collection and maintenance of grapevine samples

In the vineyard fields at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI), New Delhi, a survey was undertaken. Grapevine leaves with and without symptoms, including those with symptoms like yellowing, speckles, leaf curling, and reddening of the leaves (new apical leaves), were gathered from various genotypes in all places. For further investigation, they were stored in plastic bags in a deep freezer set at – 80 °C. The glasshouse-maintained grapevine plants were examined for all viroids and served as both positive and negative controls in all of the studies (Fig. 1).
RNA extraction and RPA primer designing

According to the instructions provided by MacKenzie et al. in 1997, RNA was mined using a Qiagen RNeasy plant mini kit under sterile conditions to prevent RNA degradation, and the amount of extracted RNA was measured using a nanodrop spectrophotometer. Referring to the instructions from the manufacturer (TwistDx, Cambridge, United Kingdom), the primer pairs for each viroid's detection using RT-RPA were built using the sequence acquired from NCBI. Sigma-Aldrich Chemicals, Bangalore, India, manufactured the primers. Table 1 lists the names of the primer sets, their nucleotide sequence, the approximate size of the amplicon they can be used to amplify, and their locations on the viroid genome.

Regular PCR was executed using all the primer sets to evaluate primer efficiencies and specificities. For the first- strand cDNA synthesis, 500 nanograms (ng) of total RNA was used along with viroid-specific reverse primer (10 μM) and 160 U of Improm-II reverse transcriptase (Promega, Madison USA). Each PCR cocktail of 25 μL was made by adding 1X reaction buffer, 2 U of Taq DNA polymerase (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA), 100 ng of template RNA (1 L), 0.25 M of forward and reverse primers, 1.25 mM of MgCl2, and 0.5 mM of dNTPs. text: As per the manufacturer's directives, RT-RPA was performed with the Twist Amp Basic Kit (TwistDx, Cambridge, UK) and all of the primer sets used in RT-PCR in a total reaction volume of 25μL. The reaction mixtures, with the exception of the template, were made as instructed in a total volume of 50μL, combined with the relevant freeze-dried pellet, 520 nM of each forward and reverse primer, and sterile distilled water to build up the volume. The mixtures were then divided between two reaction tubes. This was followed by the addition of the RNA template (100–150 ng) and 1.25 μL of 280 mM magnesium acetate. Using a dry bath, reactions were incubated at 41 °C for 30 min. Similar RPA reactions were performed using a template of 2 micro litres of unprocessed leaf sap. After being incubated at 65 °C over 10 min, 5 μl of RPA product

and 2 μl of 6X loading dye were combined (Fermentas Life Sciences, Ontario, Canada) and sorted on a 2% agarose gel in Tris EDTA (TAE) comprising ethidium bromide. The molecular marker was a 100 bp DNA ladder from Fermentas Life Sciences in Ontario, Canada. Serial dilutions of RNA were used to investigate the detection sensitivity efficacy of RT-RPA and PCR. Using healthy RNA, the RNA collected from the infected grape leaf was serially diluted up to 10−6 times starting at a concentration of 100 ng/l. Similarly, ten-fold serial dilutions of crude leaf extracts made in 0.5 M NaOH: EDTA were used to examine the various dilutions in RT-RPA and PCR experiments. RT-RPA was used to analyse each diluted template following previously described protocol. Additionally, using pure RNA from each of the four viroids, cross-reaction tests were used to evaluate the specificity of each of the four primer pairs used in RPA.

To further streamline the rapid diagnostic protocol for the detection of viroids, crude leaf extract of grapevine samples was prepared. Two μl of plant extract obtained upon crushing 200 mg of leaf sample in NaOH: EDTA buffer was utilised as a template in addition to 1.25 μl MgAc in the reaction mix prepared using the lyophilized pellet. The prepared mix was incubated at 41 °C for 30 min., followed by an incubation of 10 min. at 65 °C. An amplification of the desired size of around 301 bp was obtained for all the positive samples (Fig. 3).

In this work, 119 grapevine samples representing 22 genotypes were examined for the existence of grapevine viroids; fifteen of these samples were discovered to harbour one or more viroids. Only one viroid was found in genotypes such Chardonnay (GYSVd-1); JM, Syrah (AGVd); and Anab-e-shahi (HSVd). The RPA assay revealed the presence of all four viroids in Thompson seedless (TS), Sharad seedless (SS), and Black prince (BP) (eight samples each), producing amplicons of the predicted size. In both RT-PCR and RT-RPA tests, none of the viroids was detected in the seven cultivars Tempronillo, Syrah Rep 1, Syrah Rep 2, Black Muscat (BM), Bharat early*Syrah, Bharat Early (BE), and Beauty Seedless (BS). The most recent isothermal diagnostic technique, known as RPA, eliminates the need for pricey thermal cycler equipment while saving time and manpower. One of the RPA versions is RT-RPA, which eliminates the requirement for cDNA synthesis from pure RNA prior to amplification and allows for the direct detection of RNA viruses and viroids using purified RNA or crude leaf extract as the template. In the present investigation, we aimed at detecting grapevine viroids using RT-RPA. Our research showed that primers created for RPA performed admirably in RNA- based RT-RPA as well as RT-PCR. Using RNA as the template, RT-RPA was successfully standardised to detect all four viroids and was equivalent to RT-PCR. 71% of 119 grape leaf samples from diverse locales, representing various genotypes, tested positive for one or more viroids. This suggests that viroids are widely present in grape genotypes. Additionally, three genotypes (TS, SS, and BP) tested positive for all four viroids, while genotypes (BS, Tempranillo, BM, BE, Syrah accessions, and cross of BE and Syrah) tested negative for all four viroids in both RT-PCR and RT-RPA. Among the four viroids, HSVd was found to be the most frequently infectious in grapevine

Using crude leaf extract as the template, PCR failed to produce detectable amplicons in the presence of plant contaminants, whereas RPA succeeded but with slight compromise in sensitivity. We made an effort to extract the leaf sap using various extraction buffers, including the Mackenzie buffer, Bio Reba buffer, GEB3 buffer, and NaOH: EDTA buffer at 1:1 and 2:1 ratios (data not shown), in an effort to improve the RPA-based diagnostics. NaOH: EDTA was one of the extraction buffers that worked well for the RT-RPA test when GYSVd-2 was involved in the investigation. The effectiveness of RT-RPA utilising crude sap as the template was on par with RT-PCR and RT-RPA using RNA. Up to a 10−3 times dilution of the grapevine leaf crude extract, RT-RPA could still detect GYSVd-2. Our findings on the RT-RPA's sensitivity of detection of all four viroids were comparable to those found in transcripts of two RNA plant viruses (Mekuria et al. 2014; Srivastava et al. 2019). All the earlier attempts of grapevine viroid detection have been using PCR and thus this study helps in rapid and easy diagnosis of viroids (Hajizadeh et al. 2012). Because PCR depends on cDNA that is recovered from comparatively purified RNA for RNA viruses and viroids, the cost of extraction and amplification using RT-RPA and RNA as a template was less than that of PCR. The capacity of RPA to detect viroid using crude extracts, as discovered for GYSVd- 2, compensated for the reagent costs used for RT-RPA amplification. The RT-RPA assay takes less time overall than PCR (which takes 7–8 h to complete), is simpler than RT-PCR, and does not require the use of a thermal cycler or cDNA synthesis. According to this study, quicker and less expensive techniques could also be utilised to provide respectable findings. These techniques include heating the sample or adding SDS for brighter bands (Kapoor et al.

We showed that, as a result of the numerous modifications made, with comparable or lower costs, quicker turnaround times, adequate sensitivity, and no loss of specificity or flexibility for usage in downstream applications, RPA
can be employed as a plant pathogen detection test.

RPA's detection of all four viroids was superior in terms of downstream applications and comparable in terms of sensitivity, specificity, thermocycler independence, and speed to results reported using LAMP, another isothermal assay (Kuan et al. 2010; Almasi et al. 2013). RPA offers a substantial advancement in molecular diagnostic tools and has a great chance of being adopted by diagnostic service labs all over the world, particularly those with bare-bones infrastructure and no access to thermocyclers. With just slight modifications to primers originally intended for use in PCR, pathogen-specific assays for the detection of plant viruses can be easily created utilising RPA (Euler et al. 2013; Daher et al. 2014; Ahmed et al. 2014). RPA can also be tweaked for detection in microfluidic and solid-phase devices (Zanoli and Spoto 2012; Kersting et al. 2014) and with the addition of a RT step, can be employed for RNA templates (Ivanov et al. 2020; Lee et al. 2020; Kim et al. 2021; Kovalskaya and Hammond 2022). On combining the CRISPR/Cas13a with RPA, visual detection of the target using crude extract can be carried out on field making it the
most effective latest detection modification (Jiao et al. 2021).

As a result, RT-RPA can be used to index grapevine viroids as a new diagnostic technique and can be implemented for the quick detection of grapevine viroids in laboratories with limited resources, as well as in national and international
